[IMPORTANT: User invoked the "grilling" skill; follow its instructions. Full skill below.]

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

---

# Plan: rate limiting for the orders API

One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

content.name: ask

questions.question: What do we key the limit on: x-customer-id, client IP, or both?

brief.where: src/server.ts:5-8 reads `x-customer-id` off the request and 401s only when it is absent. Nothing verifies it: no signature, no auth middleware, no lookup. 3 instances sit behind a round-robin LB, so the observed client IP is the LB's, not the caller's, unless the LB sets X-Forwarded-For. PLAN.md line 14 lists the key as undecided.
brief.what: The header is client-controlled, so a customer-id-only limiter is one loop away from being bypassed by rotating IDs; an IP-only limiter cannot express per-customer entitlements, collapses shared NAT/proxy egress, and — behind the LB — may key every request to the same address. Which identity is authoritative, and what stops a spoofed identity from buying a fresh bucket?
brief.how: Determines the counter key, who can evade, and whether limits survive a header change. Choosing 'customer id only' is only defensible if something upstream authenticates it; nothing in this repo does.

options.label: Customer id as the contractual limit, plus a looser per-IP ceiling
options.description: Two buckets per request: `cc:{customerId}` at the entitlement rate, `ip:{addr}` at a high abuse rate that only catches header rotation.
options.tradeoff: Costs one extra Redis round trip (both in the same Lua script, so one RTT); blocks both spoofing and read floods from one host.
options.holds_when: The LB forwards a trustworthy client address.
options.cost: Needs X-Forwarded-For handling and one documented constant for the IP ceiling.

options.label: Customer id only
options.description: Single bucket on `x-customer-id`.
options.tradeoff: Simplest and matches the entitlement model, but any client can mint unlimited buckets by changing one header value.
options.holds_when: You accept spoofing risk this week and close it when auth lands.

options.label: Client IP only
options.description: Single bucket on the socket/forwarded address.
options.tradeoff: Not spoofable by header, but breaks scripted enterprise integrations behind shared egress and cannot express per-customer contracts.
options.holds_when: All real traffic comes from distinct, stable addresses.

options.label: Both must pass
options.description: Customer bucket and IP bucket enforced at the same severity.
options.tradeoff: Hardest to evade, but one noisy customer behind a shared NAT throttles its neighbours at that NAT's IP.
options.holds_when: Customers do not share egress addresses.

risks: If the LB does not set X-Forwarded-For, the IP bucket keys all traffic to one address and takes the whole API down.

questions.question: Which algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket?

brief.where: PLAN.md:10 says ~20 enterprise customers run scripted integrations that legitimately burst; PLAN.md:3 says the incident was 40,000 POSTs in 10 minutes (~66/s sustained). No limiter code exists yet.
brief.what: Fixed window permits 2x the limit across a boundary and punishes a burst that straddles it. Sliding-window log is exact but stores one entry per request — at 66/s per abuser that is ~4k entries per customer per minute. Token bucket is the only one with an explicit burst parameter separate from the sustained rate, which is exactly the enterprise shape: high burst, moderate average.
brief.how: Sets what the numbers mean later (rate + burst vs rate per window), and how much state Redis holds per key.

options.label: Token bucket
options.description: Capacity = burst, refill = sustained rate, one hash per key (`tokens`, `ts`).
options.tradeoff: Two numbers per tier instead of one, but bursts pass and sustained abuse is still capped.
options.holds_when: You want scripted integrations to burst without raising their average rate.
options.cost: Lua script arithmetic; clock is Redis TIME, not the app's.

options.label: Sliding window counter
options.description: Weighted interpolation of the current and previous fixed window.
options.tradeoff: One number per tier and smooth at the boundary, but no separate burst allowance.
options.holds_when: A single `N per minute` number is all you want to publish.

options.label: Fixed window
options.description: `INCR` + `EXPIRE` on `key:{window}`.
options.tradeoff: Cheapest possible script, but an attacker gets 2x per boundary and a legit burst can trip it.
options.holds_when: Precision does not matter and you want the smallest code path.

options.label: Sliding window log
options.description: Sorted set of timestamps per key, trimmed on read.
options.tradeoff: Exact, but per-request state grows with traffic and the hot path gets heavier under exactly the load you are defending against.
options.holds_when: Limits are tiny (single-digit per minute).

risks: Burst capacity set too high just relocates the incident; the burst number needs the same review as the rate.

questions.question: Where do counters live: Redis or each instance's memory?

brief.where: src/db.ts:4 holds one Postgres connection shared by every instance. PLAN.md:8 says a Redis 7 cluster already serves sessions for another service and may be used. There is no package.json, no Redis client, and no config file in the repo.
brief.what: With 3 instances behind round-robin, an in-memory counter enforces 3x the intended limit and enforces it unevenly as the LB rotates; it also makes the limit invisible from outside the process. Redis gives one authoritative number and one place to inspect, but adds a network dependency on the path of every POST.
brief.how: Fixes whether the limit is a real ceiling, and whether the fail-mode question exists at all.

options.label: Redis, existing cluster, dedicated key prefix
options.description: `orders-rl:*` keys, single Lua script, TTL-bounded, no reuse of session keys or DB index if avoidable.
options.tradeoff: One authoritative limit and global visibility; adds a per-request RTT and a new dependency on shared infrastructure you do not own.
options.holds_when: The cluster tolerates a new workload and you can get a namespace/quota agreed.
options.cost: New client dependency, connection handling, key-prefix and eviction policy review.

options.label: Per-instance memory
options.description: Module-level Map, swept on an interval.
options.tradeoff: No new dependency and no network hop, but the effective limit is 3x and users see inconsistent 429s as the LB rotates.
options.holds_when: You can set instance count to 1 or divide every limit by 3.

options.label: Postgres
options.description: Counter table with an upsert per request.
options.tradeoff: Reuses existing infrastructure, but puts a write on the same database as the expensive call you are protecting.
options.holds_when: Write volume is negligible.

options.label: Memory at the edge, Redis as source of truth
options.description: Local pre-check to shed obvious abuse, Redis for the authoritative count.
options.tradeoff: Best latency under attack, two code paths to keep consistent and test.
options.holds_when: You have time to build and test both paths this week.

risks: Sharing a Redis cluster owned by another service means their eviction or failover policy becomes your outage.

questions.question: Which endpoints does the limiter cover: POST /orders only, or GET /orders too?

brief.where: src/server.ts:10-16 handles POST (write, src/orders.ts:10-14 does an insert) and GET (src/orders.ts:16-18 does a select). PLAN.md:9 calls POST expensive and GET cheap; PLAN.md:3's incident was a POST flood.
brief.what: Limiting only POST leaves a polling integration free to hammer GET, which still costs a Postgres query per call and shares the connection pool with the writes you are trying to protect. Limiting both with one budget would make a read-heavy integration look like an abuser.
brief.how: Determines how many buckets per key and whether the entitlement table needs one number or two.

options.label: Both, separate budgets per class
options.description: POST strict; GET generous but finite; one limiter, two tier entries.
options.tradeoff: Closes the read-flood hole; needs two numbers per customer instead of one.
options.holds_when: You want the API capped as a whole this week.
options.cost: Roughly one extra config field and one extra bucket key per request.

options.label: POST /orders only
options.description: Match the incident exactly.
options.tradeoff: Smallest change and zero risk to read-only integrations, but GET remains an unbounded amplifier against Postgres.
options.holds_when: Read traffic is genuinely off the critical path.

options.label: All endpoints, one shared budget
options.description: Every request consumes the same bucket.
options.tradeoff: Simplest mental model, but a chatty GET integration burns the budget it needs for writes.
options.holds_when: Clients do not mix read and write traffic.

risks: Adding GET to the limiter is a new way to 429 an integration that has never been limited before.

questions.question: How do enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers?

brief.where: PLAN.md:10 says ~20 enterprise customers burst legitimately; PLAN.md:18 asks exactly this. Nothing in the repo reads customer tier, contract, or config — there is no config file at all.
brief.what: Twenty is small enough that a checked-in map is auditable and ships this week. A database column is the right long-term home for a contractual number, but it puts a read on the hot path unless cached, and it needs a tool for the owning team. A value supplied by the client in a header is not a decision, it is a vulnerability. The ownership half matters as much as the mechanism: whichever team signs the contract must be able to change the number without a deploy.
brief.how: Decides the lookup on every request, who can raise a limit at 2am, and whether a limit change needs a release.

options.label: Checked-in config map, ops-owned
options.description: `LIMITS` map in a config module: default tier plus ~20 explicit overrides, reviewed in PR.
options.tradeoff: Ships today, fully auditable in git, no hot-path lookup; a limit change needs a deploy and the numbers live away from the contract.
options.holds_when: Volume is 20 customers and changes are rare.
options.cost: One config file; a documented PR process.

options.label: Postgres table, support/sales-owned
options.description: `customer_limits(customer_id, tier, rate, burst)` read once per request or cached 60s.
options.tradeoff: Right ownership and no deploy to change a number; adds a lookup and an internal tool you do not have yet.
options.holds_when: Limits change often or are negotiated per deal.
options.cost: Migration, cache with TTL and invalidation, internal editing surface.

options.label: Tier column only, no per-customer rows
options.description: Free/pro/enterprise tiers; enterprise is one generous number for all 20.
options.tradeoff: No per-customer bookkeeping, but the loudest enterprise customer sets the tier's practical ceiling.
options.holds_when: All 20 contracts specify comparable volume.

options.label: Client-supplied limit header
options.description: Integrations declare their own budget.
options.tradeoff: Trivial to implement and trivially bypassed.
options.holds_when: Never.

risks: A silent default tier that is lower than today's unthrottled behaviour breaks integrations before any override list is complete.

questions.question: What does a rejected client see?

brief.where: src/server.ts currently returns plain-text bodies with 401/404 and `Response.json` for success. No error envelope, no rate-limit headers, no client SDK in the repo.
brief.what: A 429 without a machine-readable retry hint makes a scripted integration retry immediately and amplifies the incident. A 429 with `Retry-After` plus a JSON error code lets well-behaved scripts back off; limit headers on success let them self-pace before they ever get rejected. The alternative — connection drop or 503 — is indistinguishable from an outage and triggers client-side alerting.
brief.how: Sets the contract the 20 scripted integrations consume, and whether a retry loop can be written against it.

options.label: 429 + Retry-After + JSON error + RateLimit headers on every response
options.description: `{error:"rate_limited", retryAfterMs}` body, integer `Retry-After`, `RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset` on success and rejection.

questions.question: What do we key the limit on: x-customer-id, client IP, or both?

brief.where: src/server.ts:5-8 reads `x-customer-id` off the request and 401s only when it is absent. Nothing verifies it: no signature, no auth middleware, no lookup. 3 instances sit behind a round-robin LB, so the observed client IP is the LB's, not the caller's, unless the LB sets X-Forwarded-For. PLAN.md line 14 lists the key as undecided.
brief.what: The header is client-controlled, so a customer-id-only limiter is one loop away from being bypassed by rotating IDs; an IP-only limiter cannot express per-customer entitlements, collapses shared NAT/proxy egress, and — behind the LB — may key every request to the same address. Which identity is authoritative, and what stops a spoofed identity from buying a fresh bucket?
brief.how: Determines the counter key, who can evade, and whether limits survive a header change. Choosing 'customer id only' is only defensible if something upstream authenticates it; nothing in this repo does.

options.label: Customer id as the contractual limit, plus a looser per-IP ceiling
options.description: Two buckets per request: `cc:{customerId}` at the entitlement rate, `ip:{addr}` at a high abuse rate that only catches header rotation.
options.tradeoff: Costs one extra Redis round trip (both in the same Lua script, so one RTT); blocks both spoofing and read floods from one host.
options.holds_when: The LB forwards a trustworthy client address.
options.cost: Needs X-Forwarded-For handling and one documented constant for the IP ceiling.

options.label: Customer id only
options.description: Single bucket on `x-customer-id`.
options.tradeoff: Simplest and matches the entitlement model, but any client can mint unlimited buckets by changing one header value.
options.holds_when: You accept spoofing risk this week and close it when auth lands.

options.label: Client IP only
options.description: Single bucket on the socket/forwarded address.
options.tradeoff: Not spoofable by header, but breaks scripted enterprise integrations behind shared egress and cannot express per-customer contracts.
options.holds_when: All real traffic comes from distinct, stable addresses.

options.label: Both must pass
options.description: Customer bucket and IP bucket enforced at the same severity.
options.tradeoff: Hardest to evade, but one noisy customer behind a shared NAT throttles its neighbours at that NAT's IP.
options.holds_when: Customers do not share egress addresses.

risks: If the LB does not set X-Forwarded-For, the IP bucket keys all traffic to one address and takes the whole API down.

questions.question: Which algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket?

brief.where: PLAN.md:10 says ~20 enterprise customers run scripted integrations that legitimately burst; PLAN.md:3 says the incident was 40,000 POSTs in 10 minutes (~66/s sustained). No limiter code exists yet.
brief.what: Fixed window permits 2x the limit across a boundary and punishes a burst that straddles it. Sliding-window log is exact but stores one entry per request — at 66/s per abuser that is ~4k entries per customer per minute. Token bucket is the only one with an explicit burst parameter separate from the sustained rate, which is exactly the enterprise shape: high burst, moderate average.
brief.how: Sets what the numbers mean later (rate + burst vs rate per window), and how much state Redis holds per key.

options.label: Token bucket
options.description: Capacity = burst, refill = sustained rate, one hash per key (`tokens`, `ts`).
options.tradeoff: Two numbers per tier instead of one, but bursts pass and sustained abuse is still capped.
options.holds_when: You want scripted integrations to burst without raising their average rate.
options.cost: Lua script arithmetic; clock is Redis TIME, not the app's.

options.label: Sliding window counter
options.description: Weighted interpolation of the current and previous fixed window.
options.tradeoff: One number per tier and smooth at the boundary, but no separate burst allowance.
options.holds_when: A single `N per minute` number is all you want to publish.

options.label: Fixed window
options.description: `INCR` + `EXPIRE` on `key:{window}`.
options.tradeoff: Cheapest possible script, but an attacker gets 2x per boundary and a legit burst can trip it.
options.holds_when: Precision does not matter and you want the smallest code path.

options.label: Sliding window log
options.description: Sorted set of timestamps per key, trimmed on read.
options.tradeoff: Exact, but per-request state grows with traffic and the hot path gets heavier under exactly the load you are defending against.
options.holds_when: Limits are tiny (single-digit per minute).

risks: Burst capacity set too high just relocates the incident; the burst number needs the same review as the rate.

questions.question: Where do counters live: Redis or each instance's memory?

brief.where: src/db.ts:4 holds one Postgres connection shared by every instance. PLAN.md:8 says a Redis 7 cluster already serves sessions for another service and may be used. There is no package.json, no Redis client, and no config file in the repo.
brief.what: With 3 instances behind round-robin, an in-memory counter enforces 3x the intended limit and enforces it unevenly as the LB rotates; it also makes the limit invisible from outside the process. Redis gives one authoritative number and one place to inspect, but adds a network dependency on the path of every POST.
brief.how: Fixes whether the limit is a real ceiling, and whether the fail-mode question exists at all.

options.label: Redis, existing cluster, dedicated key prefix
options.description: `orders-rl:*` keys, single Lua script, TTL-bounded, no reuse of session keys or DB index if avoidable.
options.tradeoff: One authoritative limit and global visibility; adds a per-request RTT and a new dependency on shared infrastructure you do not own.
options.holds_when: The cluster tolerates a new workload and you can get a namespace/quota agreed.
options.cost: New client dependency, connection handling, key-prefix and eviction policy review.

options.label: Per-instance memory
options.description: Module-level Map, swept on an interval.
options.tradeoff: No new dependency and no network hop, but the effective limit is 3x and users see inconsistent 429s as the LB rotates.
options.holds_when: You can set instance count to 1 or divide every limit by 3.

options.label: Postgres
options.description: Counter table with an upsert per request.
options.tradeoff: Reuses existing infrastructure, but puts a write on the same database as the expensive call you are protecting.
options.holds_when: Write volume is negligible.

options.label: Memory at the edge, Redis as source of truth
options.description: Local pre-check to shed obvious abuse, Redis for the authoritative count.
options.tradeoff: Best latency under attack, two code paths to keep consistent and test.
options.holds_when: You have time to build and test both paths this week.

risks: Sharing a Redis cluster owned by another service means their eviction or failover policy becomes your outage.

questions.question: Which endpoints does the limiter cover: POST /orders only, or GET /orders too?

brief.where: src/server.ts:10-16 handles POST (write, src/orders.ts:10-14 does an insert) and GET (src/orders.ts:16-18 does a select). PLAN.md:9 calls POST expensive and GET cheap; PLAN.md:3's incident was a POST flood.
brief.what: Limiting only POST leaves a polling integration free to hammer GET, which still costs a Postgres query per call and shares the connection pool with the writes you are trying to protect. Limiting both with one budget would make a read-heavy integration look like an abuser.
brief.how: Determines how many buckets per key and whether the entitlement table needs one number or two.

options.label: Both, separate budgets per class
options.description: POST strict; GET generous but finite; one limiter, two tier entries.
options.tradeoff: Closes the read-flood hole; needs two numbers per customer instead of one.
options.holds_when: You want the API capped as a whole this week.
options.cost: Roughly one extra config field and one extra bucket key per request.

options.label: POST /orders only
options.description: Match the incident exactly.
options.tradeoff: Smallest change and zero risk to read-only integrations, but GET remains an unbounded amplifier against Postgres.
options.holds_when: Read traffic is genuinely off the critical path.

options.label: All endpoints, one shared budget
options.description: Every request consumes the same bucket.
options.tradeoff: Simplest mental model, but a chatty GET integration burns the budget it needs for writes.
options.holds_when: Clients do not mix read and write traffic.

risks: Adding GET to the limiter is a new way to 429 an integration that has never been limited before.
